**There is no supported way I could verify to capture this existing Windows controller session into the Zo checkout under the current constraints.** Re-enabling Entire on Zo would not capture this conversation.

Verified through supported metadata interfaces:

| Location | CLI | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Zo, `/home/workspace/Projects/vivary-issue156` | Entire **0.10.6**, linux/amd64 | `enabled:false`, no active sessions |
| Zo agent integrations | Same version | Codex and Claude Code hooks are installed |
| Zo `entire session current --json` | Same version | Exit 1, “No active session found in this worktree.” |
| Windows, `C:\Users\jeffk\AIS-OS` | Entire **0.10.6**, windows/amd64 | Status reports “not a git repository” |

Installed integrations and active capture are different states. Entire’s integration model relies on real agent lifecycle events and the corresponding transcript. Git hooks attach that captured context to commits. SSH commands from another machine do not provide those agent events or the controller transcript. [Entire integration documentation](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/v0.10.6/docs/architecture/agent-guide.md)

The repository’s `docs/ENTIRE.md` states this exact limitation in its final paragraph:

> A controller on another computer that edits Zo through MCP is not a local agent session.

It further says Zo hooks cannot automatically capture that controller’s conversation.

The installed command help rules out two apparent shortcuts:

- **`entire session attach <session-id> --agent codex`** reads the actual session transcript and creates a checkpoint linked to the last commit. With `--force`, it attempts to amend that commit. It is not a remote controller bridge or a metadata-only attachment. It would cross the prohibited transcript-access boundary here.
- **`entire session adopt <session-id> --from <worktree>`** requires another worktree that already tracks that live session. Neither checked location currently supplies that prerequisite. It is not a cross-machine transport.

I did not run either command.

**Human decision required for this PR:** approve an exception to the capture gate for the uncaptured controller work, or authorize a supported capture workflow that changes the current constraints. No `enable`, hook-trust click, or status setting can retroactively produce authentic capture of this existing conversation. A future supported session in the configured checkout is the repository’s documented route, but launching one is explicitly prohibited for this task.

Before any later capture upload, the person approving setup must:

1. Check the actual push destination with the repository-prescribed `git remote get-url --push --all entire`.
2. Verify that destination’s actual visibility and readers. A remote named `entire` does not prove privacy.
3. Confirm both settings files have no overriding `strategy_options.checkpoint_remote`, and that the elected checkpoint remote is the reviewed `entire` destination.
4. Account for the shared Git checkpoint queue across linked worktrees.

Destination privacy was **not established** by the allowed status interfaces because disabled status omits its effective destination. Entire warns that checkpoint readers can access full transcript and tool content, and automatic secret redaction is best effort. [Entire privacy guide](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/v0.10.6/docs/security-and-privacy.md)

Read-only commands used were `--version`, `status --detailed`, `status --json`, `agent list`, `session current --json`, and command help. No raw session store was accessed, no session launched or resumed, and no hooks, settings, checkpoints, commits, or uploads were changed.

name: fix-ci
description: Find failing PR checks, inspect logs or external check links, and apply focused fixes
---

# Fix CI

## Trigger

Branch or PR CI is failing and needs a fast, iterative path to green checks.

## Workflow

1. Resolve the active PR and inspect `gh pr checks --json name,bucket,state,workflow,link`.
2. Inspect failed jobs and extract the first actionable error. Use GitHub Actions logs when available; otherwise use the check link to identify the failing command or service.
3. Apply the smallest safe fix.
4. Push, re-check the PR check set, and repeat until green.

## Guardrails

- Fix one actionable failure at a time.
- Prefer minimal, low-risk changes before broader refactors.
- Keep `gh pr checks` as the source of truth for overall PR CI state.

## Output

- Primary failing job and root error
- Fixes applied in iteration order
- Current CI status and next action

# Fix CI

## Trigger

Branch or PR CI is failing and needs a fast, iterative path to green checks.

## Workflow

1. Resolve the active PR and inspect `gh pr checks --json name,bucket,state,workflow,link`.
2. Inspect failed jobs and extract the first actionable error. Use GitHub Actions logs when available; otherwise use the check link to identify the failing command or service.
3. Apply the smallest safe fix.
4. Push, re-check the PR check set, and repeat until green.

## Guardrails

- Fix one actionable failure at a time.
- Prefer minimal, low-risk changes before broader refactors.
- Keep `gh pr checks` as the source of truth for overall PR CI state.

## Output

- Primary failing job and root error
- Fixes applied in iteration order
- Current CI status and next action

L135: http-cache-semantics through 4.2.0 fails to properly validate security-zeroed cache entries when processing client max-stale directives, allowing unauthenticated attackers to retrieve cached responses belonging to other users. # Computer Use

Use this skill to automate the UI of Microsoft Windows apps. It uses SendInput, UI Automation, and Windows.Graphics.Capture screenshots that work even when windows are occluded.

If this plugin is available, read this entire `SKILL.md` once before Windows automation work, before saying Computer Use is unavailable, and before falling back to other Windows automation.

Start with the directions in the Initialize section below. Read these bundled Markdown files relative to this `SKILL.md` when you need information about the specific topic they cover:

- `../../docs/guidance.md`: core runtime behavior, target-window workflow, screenshot handling, and recovery guidance. You MUST read this before controlling Windows apps.
- `../../docs/api.md`: full `sky` API reference. Read this when you need method signatures or object shapes.
- `../../docs/confirmations.md`: you MUST read this before deciding whether a Windows UI action needs confirmation

## Initialize

The bundled `cua_node` `@oai/sky` package is the core entry point for Computer Use. Import it directly by package name from the JavaScript session. Do not spawn `codex-computer-use.exe`, search for the helper executable, or build a custom helper protocol client.

Run this once per fresh `node_repl` JavaScript session:

```js
if (!globalThis.sky) {
  const { sky } = await import("@oai/sky");
  globalThis.sky = sky;
}
```
# working

In-flight work. Scratch space with a clock on it.

## What this is for

Half-finished drafts, exploration, scraps, one-off scripts, notes from a session
you have not filed yet. Anywhere you would otherwise put a file "just for now".

## What this is not

Not a home. Nothing here is durable, cited, or safe. If work matters after this
week, it belongs somewhere with an owner:

| The work is | It goes to |
|---|---|
| A reusable idea or method | `Brain/concepts/` |
| Project plans, decisions, research | `projects/<project>/planning/` |
| A draft for publication | `content/<channel>/drafts/` |
| An unprocessed capture | `Brain/inbox/` |
| Code | The owning project under `projects/` |

## The expiry rule

Files here expire after **14 days**. On expiry, each file gets filed to one of
the homes above or deleted. Nothing is auto-deleted and nothing is auto-filed.
Expiry means the file is listed for a decision.

Use dated folders so age is visible without checking a timestamp:

```
working/2026-08-14/thing-im-figuring-out.md
```

Check what is stale:

```bash
find working -type f -mtime +14
```

## Rules

1. Nothing in `working/` is cited by anything outside `working/`. If a Brain
   page or a project doc needs to link to it, it is not scratch and it moves.
2. `working/` is not indexed for retrieval. Search will never surface it, which
   is the point: half-formed text competing with canon makes retrieval worse.
3. No secrets. This folder is casual by design and that is exactly why.
4. Deleting something here is always allowed and never needs approval.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve the Windows tree fallback after cleanup errors**

On Windows, if `shutdownProjectPreviews()` rejects because an owned preview tree or port remains, this marker makes the lifecycle handler call `process.exit(1)`. That child exit cancels `stopServer()`'s 15-second timer, while `packages/desktop/main.mjs` only calls `forceServerTree()` after child exit on non-Windows platforms, so the remaining preview process can be orphaned instead of receiving the desktop's `/T /F` fallback. Keep the server alive on cleanup failure until the parent fallback runs, or make the Windows parent force the tree when the child reports a failed shutdown.

When IPC disconnects because Electron was terminated abruptly rather than performing a normal quit, `requestShutdown` still reaches this Windows path and creates the referenced interval. If any cleanup then rejects, the catch deliberately avoids exiting, but no parent remains to run the 15-second `taskkill` fallback, so the server and its descendants persist indefinitely. Track whether shutdown was explicitly requested by the live parent, or add a bounded self-cleanup path for parent-loss disconnects.

Payload:
The P2 is valid. **Keep IPC open during graceful shutdown, then give genuine parent loss one bounded fallback owned by the desktop launcher.** An “explicit shutdown requested” flag alone misses a parent that dies after sending that request.

`desktop-server.mjs` currently calls `process.disconnect()` immediately after emitting `SIGTERM`. That makes normal shutdown indistinguishable from parent loss and prevents observing a later parent death.

I recommend these changes:

1. **Remove the launcher’s voluntary `process.disconnect()`.** Keep its message listener and IPC channel until successful exit or the parent’s tree kill. Node manages the IPC channel’s reference through message and disconnect listeners, so this can replace the lifecycle’s indefinite interval. [Node IPC reference documentation](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/process.html#processchannelref)

2. **Handle disconnect outside the `stopping` guard.** The disconnect handler first arms one referenced Windows fallback timer, then calls the existing idempotent `requestShutdown()`. It must arm that timer even when `stopping` is already true. Thus both initial parent loss and parent loss during cleanup are covered.

3. **Remove the lifecycle’s interval.** Retain successful `process.exit(0)` and Windows desktop failure-exit suppression. While the parent is connected, IPC preserves the root for its existing 15-second fallback. After disconnect, the launcher’s one-shot timer preserves it for bounded cleanup.

4. **At the orphan deadline, attempt exact-own-root tree termination.** Use the absolute system `taskkill.exe`, argument array `["/PID", String(process.pid), "/T", "/F"]`, hidden window, and bounded execution. If the command returns without killing the server, log the failure and exit nonzero rather than retaining it forever. Successful cleanup exits before this timer fires.

A self-tree kill stays scoped to the current server and its descendants, with no PID-reuse window for the root while the server executes. Microsoft documents `/T` as including the specified process’s children. However, its documentation does **not** establish the behavior of a `taskkill` subprocess terminating its own ancestor tree. The native Windows regression must prove that exact arrangement before accepting it. [Microsoft taskkill documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/taskkill)

The regression should distinguish these cases:

- Parent remains connected, cleanup rejects: server stays alive for the parent’s existing tree fallback.
- Parent disappears before shutdown, cleanup remains pending: server and descendant terminate within the orphan bound.
- Parent disappears after requesting shutdown, cleanup rejects or remains pending: the disconnect handler still arms the fallback.
- Parent disappears, cleanup succeeds: ordinary exit occurs before the fallback.

Use an actual intermediary parent process for the abrupt-parent test. Terminate only that parent, without `/T`, so the test does not clean up the server itself. The server’s descendant should retain the existing ignored-stdio and `unref()` arrangement. Final test cleanup must remain outside the measured assertions.

This needs no new environment flag, global registry, or repeating timer. If Windows refuses the self-tree kill, bounded nonzero exit solves the permanent server hang but does not prove descendant cleanup. Record that limit rather than claiming successful cleanup.

No source changed or tests ran.

🟢 Design review complete. Preserve IPC and add one bounded parent-loss fallback.

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
if ($LaunchLabel -notmatch '^[a-z0-9-]+$' -or $Label -notmatch '^[a-z0-9-]+$') { throw 'Invalid evidence label' }
$launch = Get-Content -Raw -LiteralPath (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "evidence\launch-$LaunchLabel.json") | ConvertFrom-Json
$application = Get-Process -Id $launch.Pid -ErrorAction Stop
if ($application.Path -ne $launch.Executable) { throw 'The launch process identity changed' }
$candidateRoot = [System.IO.Path]::GetDirectoryName($launch.Executable)
$resolvedRoot = [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath($candidateRoot)
$acceptanceRoot = [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath($PSScriptRoot) + '\'
if (-not $resolvedRoot.StartsWith($acceptanceRoot, [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase)) { throw 'Candidate is outside acceptance setup' }
$before = @(Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.ExecutablePath -and $_.ExecutablePath.StartsWith($resolvedRoot + '\', [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase) } | Select-Object ProcessId,ParentProcessId,Name,CreationDate)
$started = (Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('o')
$timer = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
$closeSent = $application.CloseMainWindow()
if (-not $closeSent) { throw 'The app did not accept a normal window close request' }
$mainExited = $application.WaitForExit(25000)
$mainMilliseconds = $timer.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds
$mainExitedAt = if ($mainExited) { (Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('o') } else { $null }
$remaining = @()
do {
  $remaining = @(Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.ExecutablePath -and $_.ExecutablePath.StartsWith($resolvedRoot + '\', [System.StringComparison]::OrdinalIgnoreCase) } | Select-Object ProcessId,ParentProcessId,Name,CreationDate)
  if ($remaining.Count -eq 0) { break }
  Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 100
} while ($timer.Elapsed.TotalSeconds -lt 30)
$timer.Stop()
$result = [pscustomobject]@{
  Label = $Label
  SourceCommit = $launch.SourceCommit
  MainPid = $launch.Pid
  CloseRequestedAt = $started
  CloseSent = $closeSent
  MainExited = $mainExited
  MainExitedAt = $mainExitedAt
  MainExitMilliseconds = [Math]::Round($mainMilliseconds, 2)
  AllCandidateProcessesGone = ($remaining.Count -eq 0)
  AllGoneMilliseconds = [Math]::Round($timer.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, 2)
  Before = $before
  Remaining = $remaining
}
$json = $result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
[System.IO.File]::WriteAllText((Join-Path $PSScriptRoot "evidence\quit-$Label.json"), $json + "`n", [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false))
$json
if (-not $mainExited -or $remaining.Count -ne 0) { throw 'Normal close left candidate processes alive' }

  log rules.

  patterns that sessions on this machine have earned, and it is short.

  behind any pattern that touches your work, and record
  `wiki_consulted: yes` in the trace when you did.

  blocks a piece of work updates its row before ending. Invisible work is
  the failure mode.

  that hit a failure, surprise, correction, or reusable strategy by writing
  one trace to `experience/raw/`. Traces are write-once, never edited.

  for a maintain pass. Run it after a rename, a retirement, or an archive
  move. It is read-only.
- Read `USER.md` before acting on Jeff's behalf.
- Never store credentials or secrets here.

No actionable findings in the parent-loss regression, with the planned **23-second fallback wait and 30-second test timeout**.

The fixture terminates only the intermediary parent, so the server loses its actual IPC peer. It clears the server’s fixture interval before pending cleanup, and the descendant has ignored stdio and an unreferenced process handle. Assertions occur before final cleanup. The after-request case waits for cleanup to start and preview cleanup to reject before terminating the parent, covering parent loss when `stopping` is already true.

The Linux replacement is scoped to `desktop-server.mjs` importing `node:child_process`. It checks the exact server PID, `/T /F`, a bounded command timeout, and actual server exit after the stub returns. Native Windows uses the real command and requires both server and descendant to terminate.

The recorded red result is appropriate: ten passes and the two intended parent-loss failures, with production unchanged.

For production, snapshotting `process.platform === "win32"` at `runDesktopServer()` entry is appropriate. Arm the disconnect fallback outside the shutdown guard. The concern about `taskkill` terminating its own ancestor tree remains a native Windows verification requirement. Linux simulation cannot establish its termination order.

No tests or mutations ran.

🟢 Parent-loss regression reviewed with no actionable findings.

Parent-loss regression is complete and stopped for review and the separate test commit.

The fixture now forks an intermediary desktop owner, which starts the real desktop-server entry and performs its bootstrap handshake. The test terminates only that intermediary, causing a real IPC disconnect. The observer has no IPC channel or fixture handle keeping the server alive.

Three new cases cover:

- Parent loss before shutdown with unresolved cleanup.
- Parent loss after an explicit shutdown with rejected preview cleanup.
- Successful cleanup after parent loss.

Native Windows cases require the server’s own fallback to terminate its recorded descendant. Linux records the Windows `taskkill` boundary and checks its exact PID arguments, then requires a real server exit. Failure cases allow a 23-second exit deadline inside a 30-second test timeout.

The final red run on unchanged `b9ef5acb` produced **12 tests, 10 passed, 2 failed**, with `TEST_EXIT_CODE=1`. The exact failures were the pending and rejected parent-loss cases. L76:    * ability to use job control on Windows versions that don't deal with
L77:    * nested jobs (prior to Windows 8 / Server 2012). It also lets our child

L162:      * Replace drive letter in dir by full cwd if it points to the same drive,
L163:      * otherwise use the dir only.
L164:      */
L165:     if (cwd_len < 2 || _wcsnicmp(cwd, dir, 2) != 0) {
L166:       cwd_len = 0;
L167:     } else {
L168:       dir += 2;
L169:       dir_len -= 2;
L170:     }
L171:   } else if (dir_len > 2 && dir[1] == L':') {
L172:     /* It's an absolute path with drive letter
L173:      * Don't use the cwd at all
L174:      */
L175:     cwd_len = 0;
L176:   }
L177:   /* Allocate buffer for output */
L178:   result = result_pos = (WCHAR*)uv__malloc(sizeof(WCHAR) *
L179:       (cwd_len + 1 + dir_len + 1 + name_len + 1 + ext_len + 1));
L180: 
L181:   /* Copy cwd */
L182:   wcsncpy(result_pos, cwd, cwd_len);
L183:   result_pos += cwd_len;
L184: 
L185:   /* Add a path separator if cwd didn't end with one */
L186:   if (cwd_len && wcsrchr(L"\\/:", result_pos[-1]) == NULL) {
L187:     result_pos[0] = L'\\';
L188:     result_pos++;
L189:   }
L190: 
L191:   /* Copy dir */
L192:   wcsncpy(result_pos, dir, dir_len);
L193:   result_pos += dir_len;
L194:   /* Add a separator if the dir didn't end with one */
L195:   if (dir_len && wcsrchr(L"\\/:", result_pos[-1]) == NULL) {
L196:     result_pos[0] = L'\\';
L197:     result_pos++;
L198:   }
L199: 
L200:   /* Copy filename */
L201:   wcsncpy(result_pos, name, name_len);
L202:   result_pos += name_len;
L203: 
L204:   if (ext_len) {
L205:     /* Add a dot if the filename didn't end with one */
L206:     if (name_len && result_pos[-1] != '.') {
L207:       result_pos[0] = L'.';
L208:       result_pos++;
L209:     }
L210:     /* Copy extension */
L211:     wcsncpy(result_pos, ext, ext_len);
L212:     result_pos += ext_len;
L213:   }
L214: 
L215:   /* Null terminator */
L216:   result_pos[0] = L'\0';

L218:   attrs = GetFileAttributesW(result);
L219: 
L220:   if (attrs != INVALID_FILE_ATTRIBUTES &&
L221:       !(attrs & FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY)) {
L222:     return result;
L223:   }
L224: 
L225:   uv__free(result);
L226:   return NULL;

L270: /*
L271:  * search_path searches the system path for an executable filename -
L272:  * the windows API doesn't provide this as a standalone function nor as an
L273:  * option to CreateProcess.
L274:  *
L275:  * It tries to return an absolute filename.
L276:  *
L277:  * Furthermore, it tries to follow the semantics that cmd.exe, with this
L278:  * exception that PATHEXT environment variable isn't used. Since CreateProcess
L279:  * can start only .com and .exe files, only those extensions are tried. This
L280:  * behavior equals that of msvcrt's spawn functions.
L281:  *
L282:  * - Do not search the path if the filename already contains a path (either
L283:  *   relative or absolute).
L284:  *
L285:  * - If there's really only a filename, check the current directory for file,
L286:  *   then search all path directories.
L287:  *
L288:  * - If filename specified has *any* extension, or already contains a path
L289:  *   and the UV_PROCESS_WINDOWS_FILE_PATH_EXACT_NAME flag is specified,
L290:  *   search for the file with the exact specified filename first.
L291:  *
L292:  * - If the literal filename is not found in a directory, try *appending*
L293:  *   (not replacing) .com first and then .exe.
L294:  *
L295:  * - The path variable may contain relative paths; relative paths are relative
L296:  *   to the cwd.
L297:  *
L298:  * - Directories in path may or may not end with a trailing backslash.
L299:  *
L300:  * - CMD does not trim leading/trailing whitespace from path/pathex entries
L301:  *   nor from the environment variables as a whole.
L302:  *
L303:  * - When cmd.exe cannot read a directory, it will just skip it and go on
L304:  *   searching. However, unlike posix-y systems, it will happily try to run a
L305:  *   file that is not readable/executable; if the spawn fails it will not
L306:  *   continue searching.
L307:  *
L308:  * UNC path support: we are dealing with UNC paths in both the path and the
L309:  * filename. This is a deviation from what cmd.exe does (it does not let you
L310:  * start a program by specifying an UNC path on the command line) but this is
L311:  * really a pointless restriction.
L312:  *
L313:  */
L314: static WCHAR* search_path(const WCHAR *file,
L315:                             WCHAR *cwd,
L316:                             const WCHAR *path,
L317:                             unsigned int flags) {
L318:   int file_has_dir;
L319:   WCHAR* result = NULL;
L320:   WCHAR *file_name_start;
L321:   WCHAR *dot;
L322:   const WCHAR *dir_start, *dir_end, *dir_path;
L323:   size_t dir_len;
L324:   int name_has_ext;
L325:   size_t file_len = wcslen(file);
L326:   size_t cwd_len = wcslen(cwd);
L327: 
L328:   /* If the caller supplies an empty filename,
L329:    * we're not gonna return c:\windows\.exe -- GFY!
L330:    */
L331:   if (file_len == 0
L332:       || (file_len == 1 && file[0] == L'.')) {
L333:     return NULL;
L334:   }
L335:   /* Find the start of the filename so we can split the directory from the
L336:    * name. */
L337:   for (file_name_start = (WCHAR*)file + file_len;
L338:        file_name_start > file
L339:            && file_name_start[-1] != L'\\'
L340:            && file_name_start[-1] != L'/'
L341:            && file_name_start[-1] != L':';
L342:        file_name_start--);
L343: 
L344:   file_has_dir = file_name_start != file;
L345: 
L346:   /* Check if the filename includes an extension */
L347:   dot = wcschr(file_name_start, L'.');
L348:   name_has_ext = (dot != NULL && dot[1] != L'\0');
L349:   if (file_has_dir) {
L350:     /* The file has a path inside, don't use path */
L351:     result = path_search_walk_ext(
L352:         file, file_name_start - file,
L353:         file_name_start, file_len - (file_name_start - file),
L354:         cwd, cwd_len,
L355:         name_has_ext || (flags & UV_PROCESS_WINDOWS_FILE_PATH_EXACT_NAME));
L356: 
L357:   } else {
L358:     dir_end = path;
L359:     if (NeedCurrentDirectoryForExePathW(L"")) {
L360:       /* The file is really only a name; look in cwd first, then scan path */
L361:       result = path_search_walk_ext(L"", 0,
L362:                                     file, file_len,
L363:                                     cwd, cwd_len,
L364:                                     name_has_ext);
L365:     }
L366: 
L367:     while (result == NULL) {
L368:       if (dir_end == NULL || *dir_end == L'\0') {
L369:         break;
L370:       }
L371:       /* Skip the separator that dir_end now points to */
L372:       if (dir_end != path || *path == L';') {
L373:         dir_end++;
L374:       }
L375: 
L376:       /* Next slice starts just after where the previous one ended */
L377:       dir_start = dir_end;
L378:       /* If path is quoted, find quote end */
L379:       if (*dir_start == L'"' || *dir_start == L'\'') {
L380:         dir_end = wcschr(dir_start + 1, *dir_start);
L381:         if (dir_end == NULL) {
L382:           dir_end = wcschr(dir_start, L'\0');
L383:         }
L384:       }
L385:       /* Slice until the next ; or \0 is found */
L386:       dir_end = wcschr(dir_end, L';');
L387:       if (dir_end == NULL) {
L388:         dir_end = wcschr(dir_start, L'\0');
L389:       }
L390:       /* If the slice is zero-length, don't bother */
L391:       if (dir_end - dir_start == 0) {
L392:         continue;
L393:       }
L394: 
L395:       dir_path = dir_start;
L396:       dir_len = dir_end - dir_start;
L397: 
L398:       /* Adjust if the path is quoted. */
L399:       if (dir_path[0] == '"' || dir_path[0] == '\'') {
L400:         ++dir_path;
L401:         --dir_len;
L402:       }
L403: 
L404:       if (dir_path[dir_len - 1] == '"' || dir_path[dir_len - 1] == '\'') {
L405:         --dir_len;
L406:       }
L407:       result = path_search_walk_ext(dir_path, dir_len,
L408:                                     file, file_len,
L409:                                     cwd, cwd_len,
L410:                                     name_has_ext);
L411:     }
L412:   }
L413: 
L414:   return result;
L415: }

L418: /*
L419:  * Quotes command line arguments
L420:  * Returns a pointer to the end (next char to be written) of the buffer
L421:  */
L422: WCHAR* quote_cmd_arg(const WCHAR *source, WCHAR *target) {
L423:   size_t len = wcslen(source);
L424:   size_t i;
L425:   int quote_hit;
L426:   WCHAR* start;
L427:   if (len == 0) {
L428:     /* Need double quotation for empty argument */
L429:     *(target++) = L'"';
L430:     *(target++) = L'"';
L431:     return target;
L432:   }
L433: 
L434:   if (NULL == wcspbrk(source, L" \t\"")) {
L435:     /* No quotation needed */
L436:     wcsncpy(target, source, len);
L437:     target += len;
L438:     return target;
L439:   }
L440:   if (NULL == wcspbrk(source, L"\"\\")) {
L441:     /*
L442:      * No embedded double quotes or backlashes, so I can just wrap
L443:      * quote marks around the whole thing.
L444:      */
L445:     *(target++) = L'"';
L446:     wcsncpy(target, source, len);
L447:     target += len;
L448:     *(target++) = L'"';
L449:     return target;
L450:   }
L451:   /*
L452:    * Expected input/output:
L453:    *   input : hello"world
L454:    *   output: "hello\"world"
L455:    *   input : hello""world
L456:    *   output: "hello\"\"world"
L457:    *   input : hello\world
L458:    *   output: hello\world
L459:    *   input : hello\\world
L460:    *   output: hello\\world
L461:    *   input : hello\"world
L462:    *   output: "hello\\\"world"
L463:    *   input : hello\\"world
L464:    *   output: "hello\\\\\"world"
L465:    *   input : hello world\
L466:    *   output: "hello world\\"
L467:    */
L468: 
L469:   *(target++) = L'"';
L470:   start = target;
L471:   quote_hit = 1;
L472:   for (i = len; i > 0; --i) {
L473:     *(target++) = source[i - 1];
L474: 
L475:     if (quote_hit && source[i - 1] == L'\\') {
L476:       *(target++) = L'\\';
L477:     } else if(source[i - 1] == L'"') {
L478:       quote_hit = 1;
L479:       *(target++) = L'\\';
L480:     } else {
L481:       quote_hit = 0;
L482:     }
L483:   }
L484:   target[0] = L'\0';
L485:   _wcsrev(start);
L486:   *(target++) = L'"';
L487:   return target;
L488: }

L525:   dst[0] = '\0';
L526:   if (arg_count > 0) {
L527:     /* Allocate temporary working buffer. */
L528:     temp_buffer = uv__malloc(temp_buffer_len * sizeof(WCHAR));
L529:     if (temp_buffer == NULL) {
L530:       err = UV_ENOMEM;
L531:       goto error;
L532:     }
L533: 
L534:     pos = dst;
L535:     for (arg = args; *arg; arg++) {
L536:       ssize_t arg_len;
L537:       /* Convert argument to wide char. */
L538:       arg_len = uv_wtf8_length_as_utf16(*arg);
L539:       assert(arg_len > 0);
L540:       assert(temp_buffer_len >= (size_t) arg_len);
L541:       uv_wtf8_to_utf16(*arg, temp_buffer, arg_len);

L543:       if (verbatim_arguments) {

L555:     uv__free(temp_buffer);
L556:   }
L557: 
L558:   *dst_ptr = dst;
L559:   return 0;

# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples

- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]

Brain patterns (16, from Brain/experience/wiki/index.md). Read the page behind any that touches this session, and record wiki_consulted: yes in the trace when you did.
- [external-pointers-survive-renames](patterns/external-pointers-survive-renames.md): a rename or tool retirement leaves scheduled tasks, runtime hooks, plugin registries, symlinks, skill link farms, `~/.<tool>` homes, and `~/.local/bin` shims pointing at dead paths, and they fail silently until an output stops. Close every move with the sweep list, test every link target, and prove the next scheduled output landed.
- [proxy-evidence-is-not-proof](patterns/proxy-evidence-is-not-proof.md): cleanup passed, source reviewed, config row present, index recently edited, a backup receipt, a `file://` preview tab, green CI on an earlier head, images in an export the user never opens, or `git status` in a folder with no `.git` gets reported as done while the live check never ran. Name the proving artifact first, bind CI and review to the exact commit, open a delivered document where Jeff opens it, and stay partial until the artifact exists.
- [verdict-before-mechanism](patterns/verdict-before-mechanism.md): a cause, a constraint, an attribution, or an audit finding is stated before its mechanism is checked, then defended on repeat. Write the mechanism and a falsifying check first, log an unisolated cause as user-reported, probe the artifact when a listing comes back empty, and narrow an over-covering rule in the file the next session reads.
- [powershell-silent-substitution](patterns/powershell-silent-substitution.md): an alias shadows a helper, `Set-Content` adds a BOM, `link:` splits on a space, Git Bash rewrites `wsl` paths, a text pipeline re-encodes binaries, `gh secret set --body` loses its quotes, and each runs without a report. Check `Get-Alias` before naming a function, write config with `WriteAllText` and a BOM-free encoding, set `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1`, upload secrets as one-line files through `cmd /c` or Git Bash and print key names on the far side, stream binaries by stdin and hash both sides.
- [other-model-claims-are-leads](patterns/other-model-claims-are-leads.md): a number, attribution, review finding, license term, deploy status, listing headline, or action constraint from another model, agent, or search snippet enters the work as fact, and the part that sounds settled is the part that fails. Settle every claim on the primary artifact (the citation, the tarball, the terms page, the listing body, the pinned `action.yml`), fan research out under one evidence contract, filter review findings by commit, and resolve two-agent disagreements with one observation.
- [first-artifact-is-the-wrong-kind](patterns/first-artifact-is-the-wrong-kind.md): the session builds the artifact its skills default to (ticket graph, Brain page, priced page, a placement under the wrong owner) and Jeff parks it the same day. Name the end artifact in one sentence, grep `CURRENT.md` and each `PLAN.md` for the request's nouns, state a placement assumption, and for a sales-shaped page ask "is this where we sell?" first.
- [gate-size-not-throughput](patterns/gate-size-not-throughput.md): finished work sits unshipped for days because each next step is sized for reading or needs a manual sandbox rebuild. Size every ask to five minutes as a numbered yes-or-no with the recommended option first, run the exact CI command locally before a gated cycle, and build the one-command runner before the second repeat.
- [peer-agent-state-from-the-artifact](patterns/peer-agent-state-from-the-artifact.md): a delegate's pause notification reads like an exit, a process start time reads like abandonment, and a clock reads like progress, so an agent re-dispatches onto a live branch, lists a live session for a kill, or reports dead lanes as running. Read `git log` and `git status` before re-dispatching, message a background agent for its state, grep a dead delegate's transcript rather than resume it, and check the parent chain and mtimes before naming anything abandoned.
- [half-applied-bulk-operation](patterns/half-applied-bulk-operation.md): a bulk move, delete, or add is interrupted by a roaming Defender lock, the permission classifier, or a sandbox lock, leaves partial state, and the retry assumes a no-op. Run bulk work per item with a failure report, a dry-run table, a per-run cap, ids written back on creation, and an idempotent rerun. Check both sides before retrying, find an invisible lock by rename probe, stage a blocked delete as a move for Jeff's script but never build an undo archive of trees that have a remote, and verify a repo move with `git status` against the pre-move capture.
- [hash-across-the-trust-boundary](patterns/hash-across-the-trust-boundary.md): bytes must cross a sandbox, proxy, or installer boundary and the shortcut is banned, disabled, or corrupting. Pin and checksum releases, stream reviewed bytes by stdin and hash both sides, prove an allowlist with allow, deny, and bypass receipts, and never carry host credentials across.
- [owner-inherited-from-the-nearest-record](patterns/owner-inherited-from-the-nearest-record.md): a brand, a website, or a second offering with no record yet takes its name, repository, design tokens, or release gate from the nearest existing record, and Jeff pulls it back. A diff against the record is the right check against a fourth brand and the wrong basis for ownership. Write the ownership line first, list each borrowed item as an explicit import or leave it open, and treat "name still open" as a valid end state.
- [inline-code-reparsed-at-the-boundary](patterns/inline-code-reparsed-at-the-boundary.md): code passed inline through a heredoc, `python -c`, `node -e`, a `wsl` argument, or a Windows path in a Python literal is re-parsed on the way across and fails before it runs. Write the script to a file and run the file, keep heredocs under about 100 lines, write Windows paths in Python as raw strings, and run `file <path>` on generated source before committing.
- [derived-file-drifts-from-its-source](patterns/derived-file-drifts-from-its-source.md): two files describe one set of facts (tickets and their graph, a palette and its contrast table, issues and the handoff, a document and its copy, a tool's README and its SKILL.md, an app's plugin list and its config file) and the hand-made one is read as current. Generate the derived file from the source's data in a one-command script that computes both directions, treat a tool's own listing as the source over its config, reconcile a disagreement toward the owner's choice, hash a copy against its source before trusting it, and verify a one-shot generator's output before deleting it.
- [check-asserts-shape-not-property](patterns/check-asserts-shape-not-property.md): a scanner, validator, lint, CI gate, or hand parser passes or fails on the shape of its input (a scope, a trailing semicolon, a theme name, a heading, a skipped job, a UTC date against a local filename) rather than the property it claims, and the verdict is read as the property. Prove the check with a passing and a failing fixture shaped like the real case, suspect the check when its verdict disagrees with a diff of the inputs, compare a filename to the clock its author used, and assert the property rather than a marker.
- [terms-before-fit](patterns/terms-before-fit.md): a repository, asset kit, CI action, or package is judged on its fit while the deciding fact sits in its license, terms, or runtime dependencies, which nobody opened. Open the LICENSE, the terms page, the pinned manifest, and the runtime network calls before praising the fit or writing the ticket, and record the deciding fact beside each keep or skip.
- [research-ends-without-the-ask](patterns/research-ends-without-the-ask.md): an income or career session ends on a scoped brief that names a test with a buyer in it, marks itself `success`, and drafts nothing that would run the test, so `BOARD.md` counts three proposals in thirty days and no buyer contacted. End every income session with the brief plus one outbound draft (a message to a named buyer, an application body, an offer with a price and a date) under the `jeff-voice` contract, sized to a five-minute yes, and record it in `BOARD.md` Money as drafted.

# Desktop process exit after normal cleanup

Date: 2026-10-02, America/Denver. Active Windows checks ran on October 3 UTC.
Issue: [#138](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/issues/138)
Candidate source: `5ce5468c95f3858dce712b89fb4fa135f916fb45`
Base: `c17a8cae993d6abb3a87c4949b2a047abb462224`

## Change and candidate

The dedicated desktop launcher sets the existing standalone process marker before loading the server. Its lifecycle exits after local-work cleanup and, on success, Nitro close. On this candidate, rejected cleanup waited for other stops before exiting with failure. Hosted lifecycle ownership stays with its host. The desktop's 15-second fallback remained configured, but review subsequently found that Windows failure exit could remove the live server PID needed by `taskkill /T`. Windows failure-fallback preservation remains pending. The [Windows fallback review](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/pull/173#discussion_r4170897427) and [owner handoff](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/pull/173#issuecomment-5964016108) track the separate correction. The successful normal-quit observations below remain evidence for this candidate. This candidate includes the merged #139 scheduler lease patch.

Zo built Workbench and packaged Windows x64 from the same clean source. The ZIP is 222,623,411 bytes with SHA-256 `d8952c3b4c141824ffb3d2d12804f1c82b5d031fb52e30ab486068946f7ae1f3`. Archive integrity passed. Metadata records `sourceDirty: false`, zero tracked overlays, and `commitMatchesPackagedSource: true`. Node is 24.19.0, Electron 44.3.0, and Python 3.12.14. Workbench output remains `prebuilt` with `sourceCommitVerified: false`. The separate clean-source build record supplies that relationship. The verified candidate is a private preview with no release publication.

## Windows observations

Normal window close requested quit. Timing starts at that request. The observer followed candidate process identities.

| Journey | Main process exit | All observed candidate processes gone |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Earlier `042dce25` idle baseline | 16,359.15 ms | 16,687.44 ms |
| Combined `5ce5468c` idle | 4,181.73 ms | 4,456.45 ms |
| Combined `5ce5468c` active scheduled run | 329.85 ms | 582.87 ms |
| Combined `5ce5468c` active webhook run | 309.92 ms | 559.27 ms |

Every combined observation ended with no surviving candidate process. These measurements establish the named runs, rather than a close-time guarantee. Before both active quits, SQLite held actual running automation and agent rows, and the local gateway recorded an open response stream. Its stream closed during shutdown.

After scheduled quit, the same run was `interrupted` with `background_automation_interrupted` and a non-null finish time. Its agent was `aborted` for `shutdown`. The run lease was deleted. The global scheduler lease's owner and expiry fields were null before and after quit. This observes #139's run-lease release at quit, without establishing its complete two-automation Windows journey.

After webhook quit, the same run was interrupted with that error and its agent aborted for shutdown. The same task changed from `processing` to `pending`. Its `attempts` changed from 1 to 0, refunding the claimed attempt. `dispatch_attempts` stayed 1 and `completed_at` stayed null. This matches Core's existing quit regression that requires a normal quit not to spend an attempt.

## Fixture corrections and verification

The first webhook evidence helper incorrectly required an equal attempt count and reported a false failure. It was corrected against `packages/workbench/tests/automation-quit.test.mjs`, in the case that returns an interrupted webhook call to the queue. Read-only validation of the recorded before and after states passed for both journeys. A control removing persisted interruption was rejected. No application fix or repeated provider call was needed for this correction.

An offline schedule-pause helper failed before mutation because its requested `closeDbExec` export was absent. Pause was not verified, and the schedule remained enabled. The webhook was created and closed before the next launch's first scheduler tick. The recorded state showed one current active webhook run and the previous scheduled run already interrupted.

The actual built server exited normally in 62.09 ms on `5ce5468c`. Three hosted application checks and 43 targeted regressions passed. GitHub reported nine jobs green on that revision, and Entire trail98 recorded one approval. Final CI on the later acceptance documentation commit remains pending and must be reported separately.

## Evidence boundary

The held Builder response was synthetic and loopback. Application startup, SQLite writes, dispatch, interruption, requeue, lease release, and Windows shutdown used the real packaged application. No real provider or tool side effects are claimed. Stuck Windows cleanup was not exercised. The existing controlled regressions did not establish preservation of the Windows fallback after cleanup rejection. That review finding requires separate regression coverage and acceptance.

Webhook relaunch and redelivery, full #139 Windows acceptance, and #140 and #141 remain separate. Historical receipts retain their named-candidate evidence. This receipt does not establish a finished desktop release. Package records, process observations, SQLite snapshots, gateway logs, and corrected validation stay private. No private host path, profile identity, credential, or raw webhook payload is included here.

The existing desktop tests already use `registerHooks` to stub Electron and import the real `main.mjs`. They do not use a VM.

The smallest behavioral regression is to **export the existing `launchServer` function and call it through that harness**. No wrapper or new dependency is needed.

For one test:

1. Stub `node:child_process` only for `main.mjs`, returning an `EventEmitter` child from `fork`.
2. Temporarily select `win32`, then call `launchServer` with fixture paths and a port.
3. Emit `vivary:desktop:bootstrap-needed`, observe the capability handoff, then emit `ready`.
4. Assert that the actual `fork` call received `detached: true`, `windowsHide: true`, the ordinary Node executable, and the existing IPC stdio configuration.
5. Restore the platform and hooks. Give the fake child no real PID so module exit cleanup cannot signal a process.

That binds the regression to the executed production launch call. A source regex would only check spelling, while driving `runDesktop` would require substantially more Electron window and session mocking.

The reported Electron comparison now supports the production detachment change: current options prevented IPC cleanup and left the descendant alive, while detachment allowed the existing fallback to remove both processes. The durable unit test should preserve that launch configuration. Native evidence remains responsible for proving the Windows process behavior.

No files changed or tests ran.

🟢 Regression design identified using the existing desktop test harness.

---
name: stay-within-limits
description: Use when long-running or parallel agent work must respect 5-hour and weekly usage limits by checking usage between waves, pausing near the cap, and resuming only when the window is clear.
---

# Stay Within Limits

Keep long-running agent work inside the current 5-hour and weekly usage windows.
Check usage before launching substantial work and between waves of parallel
subagents. If an active 5-hour or weekly limit is at or above 95%, pause new
work until the window is clear enough to continue safely.

## Core Loop

1. Run a bounded wave of work. Default to at most 3 parallel subagents unless
   the user or host gives a different throttle.
2. Wait for the wave to finish. Do not interrupt in-flight subagents just to
   save budget; that usually loses work.
3. Check current 5-hour and weekly usage with the host's usage/budget tool.
4. If either window is at or above 95%, stop launching work and schedule a
   self-contained resume when the relevant window should clear.
5. On resume, re-check the real window or block before continuing. Do not trust
   elapsed wall-clock time alone.

## Usage Signals

Prefer a first-party host usage tool when available. In Claude Code, use:

```sh
npx -y ccusage@latest blocks --active --json
```

Use the JSON to identify the active block start, current cost or percentage, and
time remaining. On wake, compare the active block start timestamp with the
previous one; a new timestamp is stronger evidence than "enough time passed."

If the tool reports cost instead of a direct percentage, convert through the
current account limit when known. For Claude Max-style 5-hour blocks, some users
prefer an earlier caution threshold around $500-550; treat that as a
user-configured guardrail, not a universal rule. The default stop rule is still
95% of the active 5-hour or weekly limit.

## Pausing And Resuming

When a wake/resume tool is available, schedule a wakeup for:

```txt
min(3600, secondsUntilWindowClears)
```

If the runtime clamps wake delays to 60-3600 seconds, chain wakeups for longer
waits. Each wakeup should re-check usage, reschedule if still over budget, and
continue only when the window is safely below the threshold.

Make wake prompts self-contained. Include:

- The remaining plan.
- The check-then-reschedule rule.
- The 95% threshold and wave throttle.
- The exact usage command or host usage tool to run.
- The previous block/window identifier when available.
- The next verification steps.
- The next wave's handoff packets, including scope, verification commands, and
  stop conditions, if delegation will resume.

## Choosing The Wait Mechanism

- Use a wake/resume tool when the agent needs instructions attached to the
  future resume.
- Use a background sleep or watcher for fixed timers and things a process can
  observe directly.
- Use cron or recurring schedules only for recurring fresh-session work.

Avoid short-interval polling for things the host will notify you about, such as
background task or subagent completion. For budget pauses, a prompt-cache miss
after a long sleep is acceptable; preserving the limit matters more.

## Reporting

If you pause, tell the user which window is over threshold, the observed usage,
when you scheduled or expect the next check, and what work remains. Keep enough
state in the wake prompt that the next turn can resume without relying on
conversation momentum.

95% of the active 5-hour or weekly limit.

## Pausing And Resuming

When a wake/resume tool is available, schedule a wakeup for:

```txt
min(3600, secondsUntilWindowClears)
```

If the runtime clamps wake delays to 60-3600 seconds, chain wakeups for longer
waits. Each wakeup should re-check usage, reschedule if still over budget, and
continue only when the window is safely below the threshold.

Make wake prompts self-contained. Include:

- The remaining plan.
- The check-then-reschedule rule.
- The 95% threshold and wave throttle.
- The exact usage command or host usage tool to run.
- The previous block/window identifier when available.
- The next verification steps.
- The next wave's handoff packets, including scope, verification commands, and
  stop conditions, if delegation will resume.

## Choosing The Wait Mechanism

- Use a wake/resume tool when the agent needs instructions attached to the
  future resume.
- Use a background sleep or watcher for fixed timers and things a process can
  observe directly.
- Use cron or recurring schedules only for recurring fresh-session work.

Avoid short-interval polling for things the host will notify you about, such as
background task or subagent completion. For budget pauses, a prompt-cache miss
after a long sleep is acceptable; preserving the limit matters more.

## Reporting

If you pause, tell the user which window is over threshold, the observed usage,
when you scheduled or expect the next check, and what work remains. Keep enough
state in the wake prompt that the next turn can resume without relying on
conversation momentum.
"}

On Windows, if `shutdownProjectPreviews()` rejects because an owned preview tree or port remains, this marker makes the lifecycle handler call `process.exit(1)`. Payload:
The source does **not support the blanket claim that detaching the server removes cleanup protection for all production children**. Verify the named process classes before adding infrastructure.

In pinned Node 24.19.0, libuv creates a per-process, non-inheritable Windows job with `KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`. Each non-detached `uv_spawn` child is assigned to that job. Therefore, detaching the server from Electron does not disable the server’s own job for children it subsequently launches. [Pinned libuv implementation](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v24.19.0/deps/uv/src/win/process.c#L65)

There are limits. Libuv enables silent breakaway, so grandchildren do not automatically remain in that job. It also tolerates an access-denied failure when job assignment is incompatible. These limits existed before the server-detachment change. A deliberately escaped descendant surviving a crash does not, by itself, establish a new regression. [Child assignment and exception handling](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/v24.19.0/deps/uv/src/win/process.c#L1016)

The repository confirms non-detached Windows launches for:

| Process | Source |
|---|---|
| Preview launcher | `project-preview.ts:584` |
| Code worker | `code-execution-host.ts:145` |
| Original Python command | `original-runtime.ts:633` |
| Codex model discovery | `codex-models.ts:114` |

For the original-runtime check, reuse [creator-hold.ps1](/C:/Users/jeffk/AIS-OS/working/2026-10-02/windows-acceptance/creator-hold.ps1). """Read only project schema metadata from the existing acceptance profiles."""
from pathlib import Path
import sqlite3, json
root=Path(__file__).resolve().parent/'profiles'
for profile in ['acceptance','issue138','issue138-final','issue138-merged','issue138-quit']:
    database=root/profile/'.vivary/workbench/auth.sqlite'
    if not database.is_file():

    db=sqlite3.connect(database.as_uri()+'?mode=ro',uri=True)
    names=[r[0] for r in db.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND name LIKE '%project%'")]
    output={'profile':profile,'tables':{}}
    for name in names:
        if not name.replace('_','').isalnum(): continue
        output['tables'][name]=[r[1] for r in db.execute('PRAGMA table_info('+name+')')]
    print(json.dumps(output))
    db.close()

# Vivary desktop

This package opens Vivary in a native desktop window and starts the existing
Workbench runtime on the user's computer. It has no dependency on Zo or a cloud
control plane. Opening Vivary requires no login or signup.

The desktop package includes ordinary Node alongside Electron. Native SQLite
modules stay on the Node ABI used to build Workbench. The renderer has no Node
access, uses Electron's sandbox, and can navigate only to its own loopback server.
See [Electron's security guidance](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/security).

## Current acceptance

Published checkpoint: 2026-09-22. The publicly downloadable
[Windows prerelease](https://github.com/vivary-dev/Vivary-New/releases/tag/desktop-preview-2026-09-22) pins source `98846706227432e26f519d1b546889261eb08ff1`.
This is the merged PR #78 source. Follow the
[installation guide](../../docs/desktop-preview.md) for extraction, launch,
runtime setup, profile preservation, upgrades, rollback limits, and troubleshooting.

The unsigned portable ZIP is 236,072,825 bytes with SHA-256 `e9c0abf09e9e5a66c1dbea9ec3e05d479829138d35372b10c90a34124d1b81a0`.
It retains development metadata version `0.0.0`, channel `private-preview`, and
prebuilt Workbench `sourceCommitVerified: false`. These labels describe the tested
artifact. They do not prevent its authorized publication as a development prerelease.

Direct Windows checks verified the native browser confirmation, Cancel without
a new tab, confirmed Chrome launch at the exact path/query/fragment, and page
interaction. Project switching cleared the old preview. Graceful close stopped
observed processes and released the listener. Restart retained the selected
project and an empty Preview. Profile backups were hash-verified before launch.

The package retains Codex integration and adoption-request replay. Earlier setup,
chooser, narrow-layout, and real model journeys remain evidence for their named
candidates. Six applicable GitHub CI jobs passed on the reviewed PR #78 fix head.
The site job skipped. Historical Entire trail-approval failures remain recorded.

A later unpublished `df4aedc` Windows package completed a fresh application-profile
journey under the existing Windows account. It showed missing-CLI and sign-in
guidance, used bundled runtimes, selected a Unicode folder, completed reviewed
existing-folder setup after an injected HTTP response loss, ran real Codex/Astra
file tools, displayed and stopped an npm project preview, reused the first
instance, and cleaned up on idle and active shutdown. Its
[Windows receipt](../../docs/product/multi-project/receipts/23b-windows-desktop-acceptance.md)
records the artifact hash, checks, and limits. Independent review accepted
this candidate's Windows journey. This does not replace the published prerelease.

The [acceptance register](../../docs/product/multi-project/desktop-acceptance-status.md)
owns evidence boundaries. Full existing-folder and managed-creation acceptance
under issues #14 and #15, upgrade/removal,
Native-provider turns, automations, and the remaining desktop/web journey stay
open. macOS remains later work.

### Earlier packaged proofs

Earlier Linux and Windows candidates established portions of runtime packaging,
the original command surface, and managed creation. They remain historical evidence.
The current register supersedes their current-status claims. Credentials are never
bundled, and a cross-build alone never establishes Windows behavior.

## Open preview links in your browser

The preview panel's **Open preview in a new tab** action opens HTTP and HTTPS
addresses in the default browser after a native confirmation. The dialog shows
the destination and defaults to Cancel. File URLs, custom protocols, URLs with
credentials, and POST requests are refused. Provider setup links retain their
existing direct browser behavior. A failed browser launch shows a copy-address
fallback. Embedded previews retain their sandbox and cannot create popups.

The September 22 prerelease includes this behavior. Its packaged Windows check
verified both Cancel and confirmed browser launch.

## Development

Build Workbench first, then install this package's locked development tools:

```console
pnpm --dir packages/workbench build
npm --prefix packages/desktop ci
```

Packaging the original runtime also requires host Python 3.12 with `venv` and
`ensurepip`. It does not require global setuptools. The first package build
needs outbound HTTPS for the hash-pinned runtime and build-tool wheels; verified
downloads are reused from the desktop package's `.tmp` cache.

Packaging captures the recorded Git commit and tracked working-tree changes
before downloads and wheel construction. Stage new source files with `git add`
first; untracked files are excluded. Later checkout edits cannot change the
captured inputs. `build.json` records whether that snapshot matches the commit.
The existing Workbench `.output` is copied once and labeled `prebuilt`; its
compilation from the recorded commit is not asserted.

Set `VIVARY_DESKTOP_NODE` to the absolute path of ordinary Node, then run:

```console
npm --prefix packages/desktop start
```

The desktop uses `~/.vivary/workbench` for its database, run history, and workspace.
Electron stores its window/browser state in the operating system's normal Vivary
application-data directory. The user installs and signs into their model CLI
separately. Native Settings shows provider configuration and installed CLI
status. Open folder uses the system directory chooser to connect a project;
Vivary keeps the selected folder and its conversations separate from other
projects.

The bounded native reproduction confirms an unresolved cleanup defect on the actual d8cb7665 Windows package. With Electron still alive, the observer terminated only the desktop server. The real Code worker, synthetic Codex CLI, original Python command, and pnpm preview launcher exited. The actual preview Node process and its ordinary non-detached child remained alive after 5,004 ms, along with their console hosts. Both preview processes came from the app's real approved preview action and the existing registered test root. No forced taskkill failure or detached preview child was used.

The recorded chain was server -> pnpm -> cmd -> preview Node -> non-detached Node child. Libuv's per-process job explains the direct-child cleanup but did not contain the complete shell-launched preview chain in this observation. The evidence does not establish that this failure was introduced by detachment versus the previous launch configuration. It does establish that the current package fails the required server-first tree-cleanup acceptance.

Proof and failure receipts were written before separate manual cleanup. That cleanup subsequently verified no recorded survivors and observer exit. It is not counted as product cleanup. Normal preview quit and active preview parent-loss acceptance remain unrun. This thread stays unresolved. Per the controller's bounded-wave instruction, runtime source remains unchanged while the next source-fix decision is handed back with the exact evidence.

No audit waiver was applied here.

## Intent

Fixes #138. The dedicated desktop server now sets the existing standalone process marker before loading Workbench. It exits after local-work cleanup settles and, on success, Nitro closes. Normal quit no longer depends on the desktop's 15-second process-tree kill. That fallback remains unchanged for cleanup that does not settle.

## Blast radius

The desktop entry gains one process marker. The lifecycle comment identifies both dedicated launchers. Shared startup, hosted lifecycle ownership, Core automation cleanup, and desktop kill logic are unchanged. A child-process regression runs the actual launcher and lifecycle with controlled cleanup dependencies. The existing workbench CI command includes it.

## Verification

- Test-first commit `abe1d52c` reproduced three desktop exit failures, with the hosted control passing.
- Implementation `223c875a` passes all four process cases, including pending and rejected cleanup.
- Removing the marker restores the same three failures at the real exit assertion. Restoring it passes all four cases.
- Independent test and implementation reviews recorded no remaining issues.
- HLDD staged review, CI workflow contract, line endings, docs sync, and diff checks pass.
- Exact-head Zo CI, GitHub CI including actual Windows output, built-server checks, and fresh Windows package acceptance are pending. The PR remains blocked until these complete.

## Docs impact

Architecture and desktop packaging docs describe exit ownership, cleanup order, and the retained fallback. Generated site documentation is synchronized. Packaged acceptance will update the existing acceptance register and a focused receipt after it runs.

## Release and package impact

No versions change. A private Windows acceptance package will be built on Zo and hash-verified before testing. No package publication or promotion to main is authorized.

## Remaining limits

Controlled child tests do not prove the complete packaged Nitro close path or Windows automation persistence. Those checks remain required. The separate #139 lane retains its checkout, Core patch, and automation quit tests. This PR needs its own human Entire approval before merge. Trail 97 does not apply. Source mirroring does not establish controller session capture, and no raw checkpoints are uploaded.

The browser does not run agents or mount a phone's files. The dedicated desktop server owns its process exit, like the direct CLI launcher. After a quit request, it waits for local-work cleanup and, on success, Nitro close before exiting. The server is detached on every platform. On Windows this lets it observe IPC loss and finish cleanup instead of being ended by the desktop process's Windows job. The desktop launcher keeps IPC open during cleanup. If the parent disconnects, including after requesting shutdown, the server allows 15 seconds for cleanup before attempting a tree kill against its own PID. That command has a five-second bound, and the server exits nonzero if it returns. Successful cleanup exits normally before either fallback. Direct CLI and non-Windows failure exits remain unchanged. The [issue receipt](product/multi-project/receipts/138-desktop-quit-exit.md) separates normal packaged observations from controlled failure coverage. Shared startup and externally hosted lifecycle ownership are unchanged.

+# Desktop process exit after normal cleanup
+
+Date: 2026-10-02, America/Denver. Active Windows checks ran on October 3 UTC.
+Issue: [#138](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/issues/138)
+Candidate source: `5ce5468c95f3858dce712b89fb4fa135f916fb45`
+Base: `c17a8cae993d6abb3a87c4949b2a047abb462224`
+
+## Change and candidate
+
+The dedicated desktop launcher sets the existing standalone process marker before loading the server. Its lifecycle exits after local-work cleanup and, on success, Nitro close. On this candidate, rejected cleanup waited for other stops before exiting with failure. Hosted lifecycle ownership stays with its host. The desktop's 15-second fallback remained configured, but review subsequently found that Windows failure exit could remove the live server PID needed by `taskkill /T`. Windows failure-fallback preservation remains pending. The [Windows fallback review](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/pull/173#discussion_r4170897427) and [owner handoff](https://github.com/vivary-dev/vivary/pull/173#issuecomment-5964016108) track the separate correction. The successful normal-quit observations below remain evidence for this candidate. This candidate includes the merged #139 scheduler lease patch.
+
+Zo built Workbench and packaged Windows x64 from the same clean source. The ZIP is 222,623,411 bytes with SHA-256 `d8952c3b4c141824ffb3d2d12804f1c82b5d031fb52e30ab486068946f7ae1f3`. Archive integrity passed. Metadata records `sourceDirty: false`, zero tracked overlays, and `commitMatchesPackagedSource: true`. Node is 24.19.0, Electron 44.3.0, and Python 3.12.14. Workbench output remains `prebuilt` with `sourceCommitVerified: false`. The separate clean-source build record supplies that relationship. The verified candidate is a private preview with no release publication.
+
+## Windows observations
+
+Normal window close requested quit. Timing starts at that request. The observer followed candidate process identities.
+
+| Journey | Main process exit | All observed candidate processes gone |
+| --- | ---: | ---: |
+| Earlier `042dce25` idle baseline | 16,359.15 ms | 16,687.44 ms |
+| Combined `5ce5468c` idle | 4,181.73 ms | 4,456.45 ms |
+| Combined `5ce5468c` active scheduled run | 329.85 ms | 582.87 ms |
+| Combined `5ce5468c` active webhook run | 309.92 ms | 559.27 ms |
+
+Every combined observation ended with no surviving candidate process. These measurements establish the named runs, rather than a close-time guarantee. Before both active quits, SQLite held actual running automation and agent rows, and the local gateway recorded an open response stream. Its stream closed during shutdown.
+
+After scheduled quit, the same run was `interrupted` with `background_automation_interrupted` and a non-null finish time. Its agent was `aborted` for `shutdown`. The run lease was deleted. The global scheduler lease's owner and expiry fields were null before and after quit. This observes #139's run-lease release at quit, without establishing its complete two-automation Windows journey.
+
+After webhook quit, the same run was interrupted with that error and its agent aborted for shutdown. The same task changed from `processing` to `pending`. Its `attempts` changed from 1 to 0, refunding the claimed attempt. `dispatch_attempts` stayed 1 and `completed_at` stayed null. This matches Core's existing quit regression that requires a normal quit not to spend an attempt.
+
+## Fixture corrections and verification
+
+The first webhook evidence helper incorrectly required an equal attempt count and reported a false failure. It was corrected against `packages/workbench/tests/automation-quit.test.mjs`, in the case that returns an interrupted webhook call to the queue. Read-only validation of the recorded before and after states passed for both journeys. A control removing persisted interruption was rejected. No application fix or repeated provider call was needed for this correction.
+
+An offline schedule-pause helper failed before mutation because its requested `closeDbExec` export was absent. Pause was not verified, and the schedule remained enabled. The webhook was created and closed before the next launch's first scheduler tick. The recorded state showed one current active webhook run and the previous scheduled run already interrupted.
+
+The actual built server exited normally in 62.09 ms on `5ce5468c`. Three hosted application checks and 43 targeted regressions passed. GitHub reported nine jobs green on that revision, and Entire trail98 recorded one approval. Final CI on the later acceptance documentation commit remains pending and must be reported separately.
+
+## Evidence boundary
+
+The held Builder response was synthetic and loopback. Application startup, SQLite writes, dispatch, interruption, requeue, lease release, and Windows shutdown used the real packaged application. No real provider or tool side effects are claimed. Stuck Windows cleanup was not exercised. The existing controlled regressions did not establish preservation of the Windows fallback after cleanup rejection. That review finding requires separate regression coverage and acceptance.
+

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve the Windows tree fallback after cleanup errors**

On Windows, if `shutdownProjectPreviews()` rejects because an owned preview tree or port remains, this marker makes the lifecycle handler call `process.exit(1)`. That child exit cancels `stopServer()`'s 15-second timer, while `packages/desktop/main.mjs` only calls `forceServerTree()` after child exit on non-Windows platforms, so the remaining preview process can be orphaned instead of receiving the desktop's `/T /F` fallback. Keep the server alive on cleanup failure until the parent fallback runs, or make the Windows parent force the tree when the child reports a failed shutdown.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve descendant cleanup when the detached server crashes**

When the Windows server exits unexpectedly before Electron—such as from an OOM or fatal exception while a coding worker, original command, or preview is active—this detachment removes the server and its later children from Electron's kill-on-close job. The existing child `exit` handler deliberately skips `forceServerTree()` on Windows, and `stopServer()` returns once the leader has exited, so Electron quits without any live root PID on which `taskkill /T` can operate; the agent or preview process can therefore continue using project files after Vivary closes. Unlike the handled parent-loss path, this child-first failure needs a persistent job or another descendant owner that survives loss of the server PID.

The bounded native reproduction confirms an unresolved cleanup defect on the actual d8cb7665 Windows package. With Electron still alive, the observer terminated only the desktop server. The real Code worker, synthetic Codex CLI, original Python command, and pnpm preview launcher exited. The actual preview Node process and its ordinary non-detached child remained alive after 5,004 ms, along with their console hosts. Both preview processes came from the app's real approved preview action and the existing registered test root. No forced taskkill failure or detached preview child was used.

The recorded chain was server -> pnpm -> cmd -> preview Node -> non-detached Node child. Libuv's per-process job explains the direct-child cleanup but did not contain the complete shell-launched preview chain in this observation. The evidence does not establish that this failure was introduced by detachment versus the previous launch configuration. It does establish that the current package fails the required server-first tree-cleanup acceptance.

Proof and failure receipts were written before separate manual cleanup. That cleanup subsequently verified no recorded survivors and observer exit. It is not counted as product cleanup. Normal preview quit and active preview parent-loss acceptance remain unrun. This thread stays unresolved. Per the controller's bounded-wave instruction, runtime source remains unchanged while the next source-fix decision is handed back with the exact evidence.
